clue.text: Pair up to hearten a merry old soul

indicators.note: to hearten is read as to put into the heart of, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme was a merry old soul
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone teams up to cheer a jolly elderly person.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme goes 'Old King Cole was a merry old soul', so the phrase stands for COLE, and UP goes into its middle: CO-UP-LE.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, both mean join two things or people together.

indicators.note: may give says the letters can be made to yield something else when rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rider might put on a first-rate performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters; 'may give' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: A centaur of Greek myth is half man and half horse, a horseman quite literally.

clue.text: Can turn into American fighting formations

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: US is the abbreviation for American

indicators.note: to turn round is to face back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Wondering whether something can be converted into American battle groups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb but is the noun, a tin; reversed it sits inside US.
explanation.definitionFit: Military units are organised bodies of soldiers grouped for combat.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old name for a friction match
second meaning: Satan, the fallen angel

explanation.surface: Someone who could take on Satan as an equal opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A match for' suggests an equal rival; instead it is a match you strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Early strike-anywhere matches were sold under this name, which is also a biblical title of Satan.

clue.text: A bad mark for the errant magistrate lacking rebuke

indicators.note: errant means straying from the proper course, so the remaining letters wander out of order
lacking says the magistrate is without some letters, so those are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
to rate is an old verb meaning to scold or rebuke

explanation.surface: A magistrate who strays and fails to reprimand gets a black mark against them.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the letters of RATE from MAGISTRATE to leave M, A, G, I, S, T, which rearrange to STIGMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of disgrace or shame attaching to someone.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to grasp or absorb information
second meaning: to make a garment smaller, as a tailor does

explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a noun, a legal agreement, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: One can take in a lesson by learning it, and a tailor takes in a waist by narrowing it.

clue.text: Community with spirit, though lacking humanity

definitions.text: Community with spirit, though lacking humanity

parts.note: surface reading: a lively, close-knit neighbourhood
setter's reading: a place inhabited only by phantoms, with no living people left

explanation.surface: A spirited village that is nonetheless unkind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' means a phantom, and 'humanity' means people rather than kindness.
explanation.definitionFit: An abandoned settlement whose residents have all left is said to be haunted by its past.

indicators.note: a crash smashes things up, so the letters end up jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A learner on an intensive training programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crash course' looks like a fast lesson; 'course' is a racecourse. AINTREE, near Liverpool, hosts the Grand National steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree is a famous English racecourse for horse racing over jumps.

parts.note: surface reading: an oil rig or a parade ground
setter's reading: boring into a patient's teeth at the surgery

explanation.walkthrough: Drilling suggests oil wells or soldiers on parade; the question mark points to the surgery where teeth are drilled.
explanation.definitionFit: The patient sits in the reclining seat at the surgery while decay is bored out.

clue.text: Not in favour of social worker taking one

parts.note: ants live in colonies, so an ant is a social insect worker
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A social worker on a case is opposed to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' suggests a caseworker, but it is an insect: worker ants live in social colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: Anti is used as a preposition meaning opposed to or against.

clue.text: What made the chicken opt for a secure road crossing

parts.words: What made the chicken opt for
parts.note: surface reading: the old riddle of why the chicken crossed the road
setter's reading: a guarded place where traffic is stopped and examined at a border or barrier

explanation.surface: A riff on the old joke about why the chicken crossed the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke asks the chicken's reason; the answer is the guarded post where a road crosses a frontier, and a chicken is a 'chick' after all.
explanation.definitionFit: A checkpoint is a barrier where travellers are stopped and inspected before passing across.

clue.text: Concentrate on providing a complete range

parts.note: to mass is to gather or concentrate together
providing means on condition that, as does if

explanation.surface: Advice to focus on supplying a full set of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like a selection of goods, but here it is a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact group of mountains forming one solid block of high ground.

parts.note: surface reading: blustery breezes, an apparently redundant phrase
setter's reading: the verb sense, things that wind or spiral, and so whirling storms

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'winds' to rhyme with 'finds': tornadoes are winds that wind round.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage tornadoes or whirlwinds are called this because they spin in a spiral.

parts.note: to iron clothes is to smooth them
to cross someone is to thwart or foil them

explanation.surface: Flattened metal foil is put to use as ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth foil' looks like kitchen foil; both words are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Cross is a German military medal awarded for bravery.

clue.text: Always be brave and don't worry

definitions.meaning: first meaning: read literally, an instruction never to be afraid

explanation.surface: A pep talk telling someone to keep courage and stop fretting.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old-fashioned reassurance, and literally it tells one never to feel afraid.

clue.text: It may be played on the lawn in summer

definitions.text: It may be played on the lawn in summer

parts.words: It may be played on the lawn
parts.note: surface reading: a garden game such as croquet or bowls
setter's reading: directed at, as water is turned on a dry patch of grass

explanation.walkthrough: 'Played' suggests a game, but water from a garden pipe is played on the lawn to keep it green.
explanation.definitionFit: A hose is the flexible pipe used for watering a garden.

parts.note: surface reading: money paid up front for land leased from a landlord
setter's reading: a rent, or split, in the earth, which leaves molten rock behind

explanation.walkthrough: Ground rent is a payment to a freeholder; here 'rent' is a tear in the ground, and the deposit is what a volcanic fissure lays down.
explanation.definitionFit: Molten rock erupting from a fissure cools into solid volcanic deposits.

parts.note: surface reading: be careful of one's words
setter's reading: literally look at speech, following the movement of a speaker's mouth

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means be careful about speaking, but taken literally it describes deaf people following speech by sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To lip-read is to understand speech by watching the movements of the speaker's mouth.

clue.text: A nut roast cooked for a high flyer

indicators.note: cooking mixes ingredients up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A vegetarian roast dinner prepared for a high achiever.
explanation.definitionFit: Space travellers fly higher than anyone, so the idiom for a successful person is taken literally.

parts.note: surface reading: the special railway carriages used by the monarch
setter's reading: a following of attendants who walk behind a person of rank

explanation.walkthrough: A train is also a procession of followers, so the monarch's train is the entourage, not the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants accompanying an important person.

clue.text: He wrongly assumes moneylender carries cash

indicators.note: carries says the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: a usurer lends money at exorbitant interest
P stands for penny or pence, a little cash

explanation.surface: A moneylender carrying cash is wrongly presumed to be something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assumes' suggests a mistaken belief; it means taking over a throne or title, as in assuming power.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurper wrongfully seizes a position, assuming power without any right to it.

clue.text: Article in paper is a hoax

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: card is a stiff kind of paper
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper article turns out to be a fake story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article in paper' reads as a news story, but the article is a grammatical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is a false rumour or fabricated report spread to deceive.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to begin tackling a task or problem
second meaning: an initial proposal or advance made to someone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Start overture' reads like a conductor's cue, but the words are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: One can approach a problem by setting about it, and an approach is an opening move towards a person.

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to issue a book or statement is to publish it

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor announcing it is time to go to press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' suggests a newspaper, but it is the thin soft kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue is thin soft paper used for wrapping or as handkerchiefs.

parts.note: SP is the betting abbreviation for starting price, the odds at the start of a race
to rig something is to fix it dishonestly

explanation.surface: A gullible punter caught in a betting fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' looks like a dupe, but it is a botanical shoot.
explanation.definitionFit: A sucker is a shoot growing from a plant's root, and a sprig is a small shoot or twig.

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters before it take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, and it also signals the rearrangement

explanation.surface: An angry book contains a shocking exposé.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' does double duty: its letters are part of the mix and its meaning, new, signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A revelation is a surprising fact made known, often one that had been kept secret.

clue.text: Very interested in the paper, say

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase and listen for a different spelling

parts.note: something in paper has been wrapped up

explanation.surface: Someone absorbed in reading the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the paper' suggests reading the news, but it means wrapped in paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapt means completely absorbed or engrossed in something.

indicators.note: a return trip goes back the way it came, so the journalist's letters run backwards

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the stock crossword journalist
a ride is a journey on a horse or vehicle

explanation.surface: A reporter mocks the trip home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return journey' looks like one phrase, but 'return' acts on the journalist and 'journey' is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride is to mock or treat with contempt, the same as scoffing at.

clue.text: He has no choice, poor chap

definitions.meaning: first meaning: from the proverb that such people cannot be choosers
second meaning: a penniless man who asks for alms

explanation.walkthrough: The first half rests on the saying 'beggars can't be choosers'.
explanation.definitionFit: A man living by asking for charity is destitute, and the proverb says he must take what he is given.
